# 3.4 - Research and Checking {.unnumbered}

In 2023, two lawyers in New York had to write a report for a court. One of them asked ChatGPT to find old court cases that agreed with them.

ChatGPT gave him six cases. Each one had a name, a date, and quotes. **None of the six cases were real.** The judge fined the lawyers and their law firm $5,000.

The lawyer said he did not know a chatbot could make things up. Today you learn to check, so this never happens to you.

:::{.agenda}
**Today's Plan** (40 minutes)

- [🔥]{.icon} **Warm Up** Real or made up? [6 min]{.time}
- [👥]{.icon} **Learn Together** How fact-checkers check [9 min]{.time}
- [🛠️]{.icon} **Try It** Check the chatbot [19 min]{.time}
- [💬]{.icon} **Talk About It** Should we use it at all? [6 min]{.time}
:::

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I can explain why a chatbot can write a fact that is not true.
- [ ] I can check a fact with lateral reading.
- [ ] I can choose trusted sources to check a fact.

- [↔️]{.icon} {{< glink "lateral reading" >}}: checking a fact by opening new tabs to see what other sources say

{{< warmup >}}

Two of these court cases are real. One was made up by ChatGPT for the lawyers in 2023. Which one is made up? How could you find out?

1. *Brown v. Board of Education* (1954)
2. *Varghese v. China Southern Airlines* (2019)
3. *Miranda v. Arizona* (1966)

:::{.answers title="Answer"}
Number 2 is made up. It was one of the six fake cases. It looks just like a real case name: two names, "v.", and a year. That is why it fooled the lawyer.

To find out, you could search for it. The real cases are on many trusted websites. The fake one shows up only in news stories **about** the fake cases.
:::

{{< learn >}}

### 3.4.1 - Why a Chatbot Makes Things Up

A chatbot predicts likely words. It does not look up each fact in a book. A fake court case has the same shape as a real one, so the fake words look very likely.

When AI writes something false as if it were true, it is called a {{< glink hallucination >}}. The chatbot does not know it is wrong. It sounds just as sure as when it is right. (You will study this more in Lesson 4.1.)

***

### 3.4.2 - Lateral Reading

Professional fact-checkers do not read one page carefully from top to bottom. They open **new tabs** and see what other sources say. This is called {{< glink "lateral reading" >}}. ("Lateral" means "to the side.")

:::{.steps}
1. Choose **one** fact.
2. Open a new tab. Search for the fact.
3. Find it in **2 trusted sources** that agree.
4. Mark it: ✅ found in 2 sources, ❌ wrong, or ❓ cannot find.
:::

| Usually trusted | Use with care | Be careful |
|---|---|---|
| government websites (.gov) | Wikipedia: a good start, then check the links at the bottom | social media posts |
| encyclopedias, like Britannica | a blog by one person | a website that sells something |
| big news organizations | a video on YouTube or TikTok | a chatbot answer with no source |
| museums and universities (.edu) | | |

{{< tryit >}}

### 3.4.3 - Check the Chatbot

Our school is named after **Frederick Douglass**. Let's check what a chatbot says about him. Work with a partner, or in a group of 3.

:::{.steps}
1. Ask your class AI tool: **"Tell me 5 facts about Frederick Douglass."**
2. Write the 5 facts on your sheet.
3. Choose 3 facts. Check each one with lateral reading. Use the "Usually trusted" sources. Mark ✅, ❌, or ❓.
:::

:::{.teacher title="Class size"}
**Small class (4 or 5):** work as one group. Each person checks a different fact. **Big class:** make it a race between teams. A team gets 1 point for each fact checked in 2 sources. A team **loses** 2 points for a check that is wrong. Speed is good. Being right is better.
:::

{{< talk >}}

AI can make things up, and it sounds sure when it does. Should students use AI for research at all? If yes, how?

:::{.frames}
- The chatbot got ... right, and it got ... wrong.
- A source I trust is ... because ...
- Students (should / should not) use AI for research, because ...
- Before I use a fact from AI, I will ...
:::

{{< further >}}

:::{.project title="Day 2: Check the AI's Sources"}
1. Ask your class AI tool: **"Give me 3 sources about Frederick Douglass."** (If it will not give links, ask for book titles and authors.)
2. Check each one. Is it real? Search for it, or look in the school library catalog.
3. Does the source really say what the AI said?
4. Sort the sources on your sheet: usually trusted, use with care, or be careful.
:::

:::{.project title="Check a Viral Post"}
Find a surprising claim that many people are sharing online. Use lateral reading to check it. Is it true, false, or missing important facts? Present what you found in 1 minute.
:::
